If the diagonals of a square increase at a rate of $4\sqrt{2}\text{ feet}\text{/hour}$, at what rate is the perimeter changing?
question.worked_solution:
Let $p$ be the perimeter of the square, and $h$ be the length of the diagonal. The relationship between $p$ and $h$ is

$$
p=2\sqrt{2}h.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(p) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{2}h) \\ \frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(2\sqrt{2}h) \\ \frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that each diagonal of the square is increasing at a rate of $4\sqrt{2}\text{ feet}\text{/hour},$ so we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}=4\sqrt{2}.
$$

Substituting this information into the above expression for $\frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}t}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}p}{\text{d}t} & =(4\sqrt{2})\cdot (2\sqrt{2})=16\text{ feet/hour}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the perimeter of the square increases at $16\text{ feet}/\text{hour}.$
